name: Adaptive Practice With Regrouping
title: Adaptive Practice With Regrouping
answer: Adaptive practice with regrouping is the use of AI math programs that adjust each problem to a student's last answer, paired with a teacher who uses the program's reports to form small groups for targeted instruction. It matters because the software gains on their own are modest, and the larger benefit comes from how teachers act on the data.

sections.body: Adaptive practice is the most common use of AI in math classrooms, with programs adjusting the difficulty of each problem based on how the student answered the previous one. The idea solves a practical problem: a single teacher cannot continuously track which students are shaky on a topic and which are ready to move on. The software handles that tracking and produces a picture of where each student stands. Regrouping is the second half of the idea, where the teacher turns that picture into small groups for the next day's lesson. The software supplies the data and the teacher supplies the instruction, so the tool supports teaching rather than replacing it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In elementary grades, programs such as Zearn adjust problems as students work, while older students may use Khan Academy in the same adaptive way. The teacher reviews what the software reports and uses it to decide who needs help and who is ready for more. A teacher might pull five students for a short lesson on equivalent fractions while the rest of the class continues practicing. The text does not give separate grade band procedures beyond naming Zearn for elementary grades and Khan Academy for older students. The routine is the same across grades: the program adapts the practice, and the teacher regroups students based on what it shows.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this evidence as real but modest. A review of 21 studies of AI in kindergarten through 12th grade math found a small positive effect overall, with larger effects when the software acted as a tutor or adaptive system (Yi et al., 2024). Another review found that intelligent tutoring helped students in general, but the advantage shrank when it was compared with other practice software rather than with no software at all (Letourneau, 2025). A mapping of adaptive learning research found that relatively few systems had been put to work on real student problems in real schools (Kabudi et al., 2021). The text also notes that a district switching from one practice program to another should not expect a large jump.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The gains from adaptive practice are modest, so a district changing programs should not expect a large improvement. The bigger gains depend on how teachers use what the software reports, which keeps the instructional decisions with the teacher. The research mapping shows that few systems have been tested on real student problems in real schools, so a tool that works in a study may behave differently in a crowded sixth grade class with patchy internet. The text advises asking vendors for evidence from classrooms like yours and using the pilot method in Chapter 4 to find out. The software provides data, and the teacher provides the instruction, so the choice of grouping and lesson remains a human decision.
